nameStory: Scenedesmus quadricauda gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'beautiful body' and 'four-tailed,' referring to the elegant way these tiny algae arrange themselves in groups of four cells with spine-like projections. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, scientists sometimes call it 'four-celled scenedesmus' after its characteristic appearance.
description: This is a microscopic freshwater algae that you'll never see with the naked eye, but it's likely swimming around in ponds and lakes near you right now. Individual cells are tiny green ovals that group together in colonies of four, lined up like tiny green pearls on an invisible string. Each colony is only about 10-20 micrometers long (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!). Despite being invisible to us, these little algae are incredibly important for producing oxygen and feeding tiny water animals.

idTips.label: Four-cell colonies
idTips.description: Under a microscope, cells always arrange in groups of exactly four, lined up in a neat row like tiny green beads

idTips.label: Curved spines
idTips.description: The outer cells in each colony have distinctive curved spine-like projections that look like tiny horns or tails

idTips.label: Oval cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are egg-shaped or oval, not perfectly round, with a smooth green appearance

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Colonies appear as brilliant emerald green specks under microscopic examination

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Colonies drift and tumble slowly through the water rather than swimming in straight lines

habitat: You'll find this microscopic algae in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, especially in nutrient-rich waters. It thrives in both temporary puddles and permanent water bodies, from sea level up to mountain ponds. Look for it in the same waters where you might see duckweed, cattails, and other aquatic plants.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms, though you'd need a microscope and water samples to observe them. Most active growth starts in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when nutrients are plentiful. This is the best time to collect water samples for microscopic observation.
seasonality.fall: Populations remain active into early fall but begin declining as temperatures drop and daylight hours shorten.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant during winter months, though some cells may persist under ice in deeper water bodies.

funFact: A single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these four-celled colonies, and together they produce a significant amount of the oxygen we breathe - some scientists estimate that tiny freshwater algae like Scenedesmus contribute up to 20% of Earth's oxygen production!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's most easily confused with other Scenedesmus species, but the distinctive four-cell arrangement with curved spines on the outer cells makes it identifiable. Remember: 'four cells with horns on the ends' is your key phrase.
contextualKnowledge: This species requires microscopic examination to identify, so it's mainly of interest to students, educators, and nature enthusiasts with access to microscopes. Despite being invisible, understanding these tiny organisms helps us appreciate the complex microscopic world that supports all aquatic life.
compareHints: Scenedesmus quadricauda differs from its relatives by its consistent four-cell colonies and the curved spines on outer cells. Scenedesmus obtusus has blunt-ended cells without prominent spines, while Scenedesmus apiculatus has pointed projections but often forms colonies of different sizes. The 'four cells with curved tails' pattern is diagnostic for quadricauda.
